guide.line: In March 1908 the Hope family crossed the Atlantic from England to Cleveland, Ohio.

guide.line: Among the seven sons was a four-year-old named Leslie Townes Hope.

guide.line: His father's first job there was carving stone for the Church of the Covenant, and he later worked on Cleveland's Guardians of Traffic.

guide.line: The boy went to the Fairmount schools and East High, sang in the Church of the Covenant choir, took dancing lessons, and boxed briefly under the name "Packy East" before losing in a novice championship and giving it up.

guide.line: Hope went into vaudeville in 1922, worked up through partner acts and Broadway revues, and in 1928 struck out as a solo comedian — changing his first name to "Bob."

guide.line: Broadway brought him Roberta and the 1936 Ziegfeld Follies; from 1938, radio brought him The Bob Hope Show on NBC.
guide.copy_md_sentence: Broadway brought him *Roberta* and the 1936 Ziegfeld Follies; from 1938, radio brought him *The Bob Hope Show* on NBC.

guide.line: In 1941 Hope entertained troops at an air base in California, joined the USO, and never really stopped.

guide.line: He took his radio show overseas in 1943, began his Christmas shows for the troops in 1948, and performed for American servicemen and women through the Korean War, Vietnam, and the Gulf War.

guide.line: Hope never took a citizenship oath of his own.

guide.line: The boy who had crossed the Atlantic at four was made an American by an act in which he took no part.

guide.line: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences records three honours for him: an Honorary Award for 1952, the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award for 1959, and a second Honorary Award for 1965, presented in the spring of 1966.
